name: Contraception methods the NHS lists compared
summary: The NHS lists hormonal, long-acting, barrier, emergency and permanent methods; they differ in how they work and how long they last.
keyPoints: The NHS groups contraception into hormonal methods, coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options.
NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible methods that need no daily attention.
The NHS lists only condoms and internal condoms as protecting against STIs, which the hormonal methods do not.
Emergency contraception is the emergency pill or the copper IUD, each with a time limit after sex.
The NHS says contraception is free, from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies.

body.heading: Which contraception methods does the NHS list?
body.body: The NHS contraception guide groups the methods it lists in several ways. These are hormonal methods, copper coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options. The hormonal methods are the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill (or mini pill), the patch, the vaginal ring, the implant, the injection and the IUS, which is a hormonal coil. The IUD, or copper coil, contains no hormones. The barrier methods are condoms, internal (female) condoms, the diaphragm and the cap. Female sterilisation and vasectomy are the permanent methods. The NHS says contraception is free.

body.heading: How do the pill, patch, ring and injection work?
body.body: The combined pill contains two hormones, progestogen and oestrogen. The patch and the vaginal ring release both of these hormones too. The NHS says the combined pill stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month. NHS inform Scotland adds that the hormones make it harder for sperm to reach an egg and thin the lining of the womb. The patch is described as working in a similar way, and it also thickens the mucus at the neck of the womb. The progestogen-only pill contains a man-made version of progestogen and, unlike the combined pill, no oestrogen. An NHS trust page says its main action is to thicken the mucus at the neck of the womb, which hinders sperm. The injection contains progestogen, and its main action is to stop the ovaries releasing an egg. The pill, patch and ring are used regularly, while the injection is repeated every few weeks, depending on the type.

body.heading: Which methods last the longest?
body.body: NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible contraception. It says these methods, unlike the pill or condoms, do not need attention every day or at each sex act. They are called reversible because they can be stopped when someone decides to become pregnant. The NHS says the copper coil lasts for years, and the length depends on the type. The hormonal coil and the implant also last for years, though sources give different lengths. The injection works for a much shorter time, in weeks rather than years. Several NHS sexual health services say fertility returns soon after an implant, IUS or IUD is taken out. After the injection, fertility can take longer to return, with one NHS-linked source saying up to a year.

body.heading: How do barrier methods differ, and which protect against infections?
body.body: Barrier methods put a physical barrier between sperm and egg. Examples include condoms, internal condoms, caps and diaphragms. They are used at the time of sex, rather than daily or over years. Condoms help prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, or STIs. The NHS lists only condoms and internal condoms as methods that protect against STIs. The hormonal methods do not protect against STIs.

body.heading: What is emergency contraception?
body.body: Emergency contraception is used after sex to help prevent pregnancy. The NHS lists emergency pills and the copper IUD as the options. There are two main emergency pills in the UK, and each works within a set time after sex. The NHS gives the limit as 3 days for one type of pill and 5 days for the other. A copper IUD can also be fitted as emergency contraception, and one NHS source says this works within five days of unprotected sex. A nurse or doctor fits the IUD, usually at a sexual health clinic or GP surgery, after making an appointment. Emergency contraception is also free from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies.

body.heading: What are the permanent methods?
body.body: The NHS lists female sterilisation and vasectomy as permanent methods. It says sterilisation lasts forever. In a vasectomy, the tube that carries sperm from the testicles to the penis is tied, cut or sealed. A vasectomy is free on the NHS, although one source notes that waiting lists can be long. Information and advice about sterilisation is available from a GP surgery or a sexual health clinic.

body.heading: Where can someone get contraception for free?
body.body: Contraception is free on the NHS. It is available from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies. Sexual health clinics are also called family planning, GUM or contraception clinics. Under the NHS Pharmacy Contraception Service in England, a person does not need to be registered with a GP. Supplies of contraception and emergency contraception through this route are free and exempt from prescription charges. The NHS website lets people find GPs, sexual health clinics and pharmacies by postcode. NHS inform Scotland and NHS 111 Wales publish their own contraception pages for those nations.
